## English in Norway: Friend or Threat?

Norway is regularly named one of the most English-proficient countries in the world among non-native speakers. Norwegians consistently rank near the top of international English proficiency indexes, and English is woven deeply into Norwegian daily life -- entertainment, social media, business, and higher education.

But this close relationship raises important questions. Is English *enriching* Norwegian, or gradually *replacing* it in certain areas? Are young Norwegians losing the ability to express themselves fully in Norwegian? And what happens to the Scandinavian languages when everyone switches to English? Consider how English already permeates Norwegian life: most films, TV, music, and games are in English; young Norwegians use English freely on Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube; many university courses are taught in English; international companies often use English as their working language; the language of computing and gaming is predominantly English; and English words appear increasingly in advertising. The key question of this chapter: is this a natural evolution of language contact, or a genuine threat to Norwegian language and culture?

## Domain Loss and the Code-Mixing Generation

A central concept for thinking about this is **domain loss** -- when a language gradually ceases to be used in particular areas of life, replaced by another. A *domain* is a social context where language is used: family, education, government, science, business, entertainment. When Norwegian loses a domain, it means English has taken over that function.

In Norway, several domains show this pattern. In **higher education**, many master's programmes are taught entirely in English, and students may never learn the Norwegian terminology for their field. In **research**, most academic papers by Norwegian researchers are published in English. In **business**, international companies operating in Norway often use English as their corporate language. And in **technology**, Norwegian lacks much IT vocabulary, so English terms fill the gap. Why does this matter? If Norwegian is not used in academia, research, and business, it may gradually lose the ability to function there -- developing vocabulary gaps and lacking technical terms. Future generations might come to see Norwegian as merely a "home language," creating a *diglossic* situation where English is the prestigious "high" language and Norwegian is relegated to "low" functions. The counter-arguments are real too: Norwegian has 5 million speakers and strong institutional support, languages have always borrowed from each other, and language planning can offset some loss by creating Norwegian technical vocabulary.

Meanwhile, young Norwegians mix English and Norwegian constantly. Look at typical teenage texts: "Omg den serien er literally so good!! har du sett episode 3 ennaa?" / "yesss den var insane. men lowkey cringe at slutten tho." The patterns are clear: English discourse markers (omg, literally, lowkey, anyway, tho) are deeply integrated; English evaluative adjectives (insane, cringe, good) carry emotional weight; and English words are slotted into Norwegian grammar. Crucially, this is *not* random -- Norwegian grammar stays dominant, English words are inserted into Norwegian structures, and it follows predictable patterns shaped by media and peer culture. And it does not mean these speakers cannot use "pure" Norwegian or English when the situation requires it; most can adjust their register across texting friends, writing essays, and speaking to grandparents.

## The Fading Scandinavian Language Community

There is one more dimension to the English-in-Norway story, and it concerns Norway's neighbours. Norwegian, Swedish, and Danish are closely related languages that are, to varying degrees, **mutually intelligible** -- speakers of one can often understand the others without formal study. All three are North Germanic languages descended from Old Norse. Written Norwegian (especially Bokmål) and Danish are very similar, spoken Norwegian and Swedish share many features, and Danish pronunciation is the hardest for other Scandinavians to follow.

Historically, Scandinavians have communicated by each speaking their own language and understanding the others -- a practice called **semi-communication**, and a meaningful part of Nordic cultural identity and cooperation. But this is increasingly under pressure, and English is part of the reason. A 2005 study found that young Scandinavians understood each other's languages significantly less well than older generations. Young Scandinavians increasingly switch to English when communicating across borders, exposure to each other's languages through media has declined as English-language media dominates, and the sense of a shared Scandinavian language community is weakening.

Why does this matter? It represents a cultural loss -- the Scandinavian language community is a unique phenomenon. It gives native English speakers an advantage in Nordic contexts. It weakens the practical case for maintaining distinct Scandinavian languages ("why not just use English?"). And it reflects broader global patterns of English displacing inter-linguistic communication. To respond, Norway relies on **language planning** (*språkrøkt*) -- organised efforts by institutions like **Språkrådet** (the Language Council) to develop Norwegian terminology and promote Norwegian use. A few terms round out the picture: a **loanword** is a word borrowed from another language (Norwegian *jobb*, *streame*, *kul*); an **anglicism** is an English word or expression used in another language; and **diglossia** is a situation where two languages are used for different social functions, one "high" and one "low." Your own language use as a young Norwegian is part of this ongoing story.
